Shotgun
SHOT-gun
interjection / noun (Gen X slang)
From riding shotgun, the armed guard who sat beside the stagecoach driver with a shotgun across his knees in the American West; the phrase was spread by Western fiction and films of the early 20th century. Later in the century teenagers turned it into a seat-claim: the first to shout "Shotgun!" wins the front passenger seat. In the Gen X station-wagon years the call came with unwritten rules — the car must be in sight, no calling it from inside the house — that every sibling could recite.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To call shotgun is to shout the word before anyone else and claim the front seat of the car. In Gen X families it was law: the first to yell it got the seat, and siblings argued the fine points like lawyers — do you have to see the car? does it count from the porch? The word is innocent; the scramble behind it is very old. The disciples called shotgun on the kingdom. James and John came to Jesus and asked, "Grant unto us that we may sit, one on thy right hand, and the other on thy left hand, in thy glory" (Mar 10:37), and the other ten were indignant, very likely because they had not called it first. Jesus answered with a different seating rule: "whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister" (Mat 20:26), and "whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant" (Mat 20:27). At a feast He told men to "go and sit down in the lowest room" and wait to be invited higher (Luk 14:10). "If any man desire to be first, the same shall be last of all, and servant of all" (Mar 9:35). Paul turns it into a habit of mind: "in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves" (Php 2:3). A family can keep the game — it settles arguments fast — but a father can also teach the better move. Now and then, let your son win shotgun and hand it to his little sister, or to Grandma, without being asked. That is the kingdom’s seating chart, and the Lord Himself took the lowest seat of all.

Webster 1828 Definition

The call that claims the front passenger seat, from the Old West’s riding shotgun; a harmless family rule over a very old scramble for the best seat, which Jesus answered by making the chief the servant of all (Mat 20:27).

SHOTGUN, interj. and n. (Gen X slang, American; universal 1970s–80s) A call claiming the front passenger seat of a car; the seat itself. "Shotgun!" "No fair — you had shotgun last time."

From riding shotgun, the stagecoach guard seated beside the driver with a shotgun; spread by Western fiction and film.

Family case law: the car must be in sight; no calling it from indoors; the loser rides in the back of the station wagon.

No entry in Webster 1828; shotgun is a 19th-century American word, and the seat-claim is 20th-century slang.

Decode for parents: the game settles arguments; the kingdom teaches a child to give the best seat away.

Key Scripture

Mar 10:37 — "They said unto him, Grant unto us that we may sit, one on thy right hand, and the other on thy left hand, in thy glory."

Mat 20:26 — "But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister;"

Mat 20:27 — "And whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant:"

Luk 14:10 — "But when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher: then shalt thou have worship in the presence of them that sit at meat with thee."

Php 2:3 — "Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves."

Modern Corruption

Shotgun is a harmless game over a very old appetite — the scramble for the best seat — which Jesus answered by putting the servant at the head of the table.

expand to see more

The scramble for the seat. Nothing is wrong with a family rule that ends arguments before they start. But the game exercises a muscle every child already has too much of: the reflex to grab the best place first. The disciples had it on the road to Jerusalem, asking for the seats at Christ’s right and left hand (Mar 10:37) while He was speaking of His death. Grown men have it in boardrooms, churches, and committee meetings. The Lord’s cure was not a ban on seats but a new definition of greatness (Mat 20:26-27).

Friend, go up higher. Jesus told His hearers to take the lowest room and let the host call them up (Luk 14:10). Paul made it a rule of the mind: esteem others better than yourself (Php 2:3). A boy who learns to give up shotgun to his grandmother is learning the posture of the Son of God, who did not grasp at the highest place but took the form of a servant. That lesson will serve him longer than any front seat.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old West riding shotgun (the stagecoach guard) → Western fiction and film → teenage seat-claim → Gen X family law; Scripture: whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant (Mat 20:27).
